title: Diffusion, meshes and Burgers: three small problems with a known answer
summary: A diffusion problem with an exact solution, a one-dimensional mesh with a stretching ratio, and a viscous Burgers wave that steepens into a shock: simple pictures for checking what time stepping, grid spacing and viscosity do to a solution.

07_mesh_zones: Uniform and stretched 1D meshes (n = 20, ratio 1.12): cell centres, faces, cell-size distribution and expansion ratio
12_burgers_shock: Viscous Burgers equation: a sine wave steepening for viscosity 0.001, 0.01 and 0.05

read_the_figure.question: Does the numerical solution reproduce the exact (or physically expected) one, and what do the mesh and the viscosity change about the picture?
read_the_figure.axes: History figure: left, time t against the largest change in phi between steps (log scale), a residual-like signal; right, phi against x at t = 1 with the exact solution dashed. Mesh figure: x for cell faces and centres, then cell index against cell size dx_i (log scale), a Gaussian drawn over the faces, and the ratio of neighbouring cell sizes. Burgers figure: x against u at four times, three viscosities side by side, with the initial sine dashed.
look_at: Left panel of the history figure: a straight line on this semi-log plot means exponential decay. The three time integrators lie on one line, so for this problem they cannot be told apart.
Right panel of the history figure: does the dashed exact curve disappear under the three solid ones? Here it does; the figure cannot rank the schemes.
Mesh figure: denser vertical lines mean smaller cells. The uniform mesh has constant cell size 0.05; the stretched one grows steadily from fine near x = 0 to coarse near x = 1.
Mesh figure, bottom row: how many faces fall under the Gaussian peak, and whether the expansion ratio stays below the stated guideline of 1.2.
Burgers figure: the steepness of the front in each panel, and whether anything exceeds the initial range of plus and minus one.
read_the_figure.proves: These figures check expectations rather than a design target: that a stable integrator at a sensible step reproduces an analytic decay, that the mesh is built as specified, and that numerical solution of the nonlinear equation shows the right qualitative behaviour (steepening, viscous smoothing).
if_wrong: Curves that separate in the history figure: the time step is too large for the explicit integrator, or the implicit solves were not converged.
A residual curve that is not a straight line on semi-log axes: more than one decay rate is active (an initial transient) or the run has not reached the asymptotic mode.
Cells that are fine away from the feature: the mesh is spending resolution where nothing happens.
In the Burgers panels, values beyond plus and minus one: the scheme produces numerical oscillations, because the exact viscous solution cannot exceed the initial maximum.
must_check: The scheme, time step and grid are stated. In the history figure the time step and the grid size are not printed; only alpha = 0.1 and the end time t = 1 are.
The y-quantity of the 'residual' is stated: here it is the largest change between consecutive steps, not a true equation residual.
The initial condition of the diffusion run (not printed; the final peak of about 0.373 agrees with a unit-amplitude half sine wave, see the computed value).
The expansion ratio is shown and compared with a guideline (it is: below 1.2 for accuracy, with the stretched mesh drawn at 1.12).
Viscosity, grid and numerical scheme of the Burgers run: only viscosity values and times are printed.
as_drawn: Values read off the figures unless computed.
History: step change falls from about 0.019 at the first plotted step to about 0.0065 at t = 1; final peak value about 0.373.
Computed check: for phi0 = sin(pi x) and alpha = 0.1, exp(-alpha pi^2 t) at t = 1 is 0.3727, which matches the plotted peak.

Mesh: n = 20 cells on [0,1]; uniform dx = 0.05; stretched with ratio 1.12, so the first cell is about 0.0139 and the last about 0.120 (computed from the geometric series), matching the cell-size plot's range.
Mesh, Gaussian panels: about 7 cells across the peak on the uniform mesh (printed); the stretched panel's title says the fine cells are away from the peak.

Burgers: at nu = 0.001, t = 0.15 the profile has spikes reaching about plus 2.3 and minus 2.3 at the shock; at nu = 0.01 and 0.05 the profile stays inside plus and minus one and the front is progressively wider.

terms.meaning: phi_t = alpha phi_xx: values relax toward their neighbours' average; each sine mode decays exponentially.
Explicit first-order, implicit first-order and implicit second-order time stepping. Forward Euler for diffusion is stable only for small steps.
The dimensionless step size for diffusion. Forward Euler needs it at most one half.
The largest difference between two consecutive time levels; a residual-like indicator of whether a run has settled.
A finite-volume mesh is made of cells bounded by faces; unknowns live at the cell centres.
The ratio of neighbouring cell sizes. Large jumps reduce accuracy.
The simplest nonlinear transport equation: the wave speed is the solution itself. Viscosity nu competes with steepening.
A jump that forms when faster fluid catches slower fluid. In the viscous equation it is a thin smooth layer, with width set by nu.
Ratio of convection to diffusion at the grid scale: central differencing needs it at most about two to avoid wiggles.

remember: Diffusion with fixed boundaries: every sine mode decays as exp(-alpha k^2 t), the lowest one slowest.
A straight line on semi-log axes is an exponential decay with slope equal to the rate.
Forward Euler for diffusion needs r <= 1/2; backward Euler and Crank-Nicolson are stable for any r (accuracy still depends on dt).
A geometric mesh: dx_i = dx_1 times r_e to the (i-1); the cell sizes add up to the domain length.
Burgers: characteristics carry u, so the profile steepens where u decreases with x and breaks at t = 1 / max |u0'|.

understand.title: Why the three integrators coincide
understand.text: When dt is small enough, all three have the same leading behaviour: they differ in a term of size proportional to dt (or dt squared) times a very small decay rate. The curves overlap to within line width. The figure is therefore a consistency check, not a comparison; the differences appear at large dt, where forward Euler would blow up.

understand.title: What the step change measures
understand.text: For a decaying solution the change per step is about dt times the time derivative, which itself decays at the same rate. That is why it falls on a straight line with the same slope as the solution. It is a stand-in for a residual in a steady solver and is useful only if its meaning is stated.

understand.title: Why meshes are stretched
understand.text: Boundary layers and fronts need small cells where gradients are large and can afford big cells elsewhere. A constant ratio keeps cell sizes smooth; large ratio jumps introduce a truncation error of lower order.

understand.title: How viscosity limits steepening
understand.text: Without viscosity the profile develops a jump at t = 1/(2 pi), about 0.159. With viscosity the front is a balance between steepening and diffusion with a thickness proportional to nu: thinner for smaller nu, until the grid can no longer resolve it and the numerical solution rings.

steps.title: Exact diffusion solution
steps.note: Separation of variables with zero values at both ends. Each mode with wavenumber k decays at rate alpha k^2; the lowest has k = pi.

steps.title: Semi-log reading of the history
steps.note: A straight line with slope minus alpha pi^2, about -0.99 for alpha = 0.1. Over t = 1 that is a drop by a factor of about e, close to the factor of about three seen in the plotted step change.

steps.title: Forward Euler stability for diffusion
steps.note: The worst mode is theta = pi, where G = 1 - 4r. This is the diffusion counterpart of the CFL limit; with it dt is bounded by dx squared over 2 alpha.

steps.title: Implicit steps are stable for all r
steps.note: Both have modulus at most one for every r. Crank-Nicolson approaches minus one for large r (it rings), backward Euler approaches zero (it damps).

steps.title: A geometric mesh
steps.note: The n cell sizes form a geometric series that must sum to the length L. For L = 1, n = 20, r_e = 1.12 the first cell is 0.0139 and the last 0.1195.

steps.title: Burgers: where the wave breaks
steps.note: Along a characteristic u is constant and the speed is u, so neighbouring characteristics cross when the initial slope is negative. For the sine of amplitude one the breaking time is 1/(2 pi), the value quoted in the figure's title.

steps.title: Viscous shock thickness
steps.note: The balance of u u_x against nu u_xx gives a layer thickness proportional to nu; the grid resolves it only if the cell Peclet number is about two or less. Beyond that, central schemes oscillate: the spikes at nu = 0.001.

analyze.q: The history figure shows FE, CN and BE on one line. What would you change in the experiment so that the curves separate, and in which order would you expect them to separate?
analyze.hint: Raise dt past the forward Euler limit; then compare errors at a moderate dt.

analyze.q: In the stretched mesh figure, the Gaussian lies where the cells are coarse. Using the printed number of cells across the peak on the uniform mesh, estimate the number across the peak on the stretched mesh and say what happens to the peak's accuracy.
analyze.hint: Read cell sizes near x = 0.5 off the cell-size plot, about 0.07 to 0.09.

analyze.q: In the nu = 0.001 panel the solution exceeds 1 in magnitude although the exact solution cannot. Name two remedies.
analyze.hint: Refine the grid near the shock, or use a bounded (limited or upwind-biased) scheme.

evaluate.q: Is 'residual-like step change' a good convergence indicator for this transient problem? What else would you plot?
evaluate.hint: The error against the exact solution, which is available here.

evaluate.q: Is the guideline 'expansion ratio below 1.2' a rule or a rule of thumb? What does it depend on?
evaluate.hint: The order of accuracy and the smoothness of the solution.

create: Add a panel to the history figure showing error against the exact solution for each integrator at a time step ten times larger.
Redesign the mesh figure so the stretched mesh is fine where the Gaussian is, and report the cells across the peak for both meshes.

checks.q: Why is a straight line on semi-log axes an exponential decay?
checks.hint: Take logs of C exp(-s t).
checks.answer: The logarithm of C exp(-s t) is ln C - s t, a straight line of slope -s. Here s is alpha pi^2, about one.

checks.q: What is the largest forward-Euler time step for diffusion with alpha = 0.1 and dx = 0.01?
For the Burgers sine of amplitude 1 and wavenumber 2 pi, when does the inviscid solution break?
checks.hint: One over the largest negative slope.
checks.answer: The steepest negative slope is -2 pi at x = 0.5, so t = 1/(2 pi) = 0.159.

checks.q: A mesh has cell sizes growing by a factor 1.3 per cell. Is that acceptable?
checks.answer: It exceeds the guideline of 1.2 shown on the mesh figure, so truncation error grows where the cells jump in size; either add cells or reduce the ratio, unless the solution is smooth there.

checks.q: How would you build a Burgers test with a known exact answer?
checks.answer: The Cole-Hopf substitution u = -2 nu (ln theta)_x turns Burgers into the heat equation for theta, which can be solved exactly for a sine initial condition, giving a reference to measure the numerical error.
